readerTitle: Sales grew 40%. The business still didn't work.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (재사용 운반 상자 제조, 선물 가게 체인) + 실제 관찰 (Marc Andreessen 2007년 에세이) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 제품-시장 적합성이 없다는 신호는 숫자보다 '노력'에서 먼저 보인다. 판매가 고객의 수요에 끌려오는지, 내가 밀어서 만드는지를 본다.
misconception: 매출이 늘고 팀이 바쁘면 제품-시장 적합성이 있는 것이다.

sources.text: Andreessen, M. (2007). The Pmarca Guide to Startups, part 4: The only thing that matters.
공장과 선물 가게 사례와 수치는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Andreessen 에세이(2007년 6월)의 내용은 직접 인용하지 않고 요약했습니다. 적합성이 없을 때의 묘사(고객이 가치를 잘 못 느끼고, 입소문이 퍼지지 않고, 판매 주기가 길고, 성사되지 않는 거래가 많다)가 원문과 맞는지, URL이 유효한지 게시 전에 확인하세요.
3번 카드 수치(10건 중 9건 창업자 직접 성사, 평균 할인 15%, 판매 주기 4개월, 추천 고객 0)는 모두 가상입니다. 서로 모순되지 않는지만 확인했습니다.
7번 카드의 '병원 등 일부 업종은 원래 판매 주기가 길다'는 일반적 설명으로, 특정 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Sales grew 40%. The business still didn't work.
body: Dana runs a small factory that makes reusable plastic crates for warehouses. Last year, sales grew 40%. Her team was busy, and the order book looked full.
Then she took a month off. New orders almost stopped.

image.label: Stacked crates in a quiet factory with an empty order tray
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 공장 안에 색색의 플라스틱 운반 상자가 높이 쌓여 있고, 앞쪽 책상의 '주문서' 트레이는 비어 있음. 벽 달력에 한 달이 통째로 표시됨. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Before you scale, what do you check?
body: Go back to before Dana's month off. You run the crate factory. Sales are up 40%.
You're about to hire two more salespeople and buy a second molding machine. What do you check first?

options.text: Whether orders keep coming when you stop pushing
options.feedback: This tests whether demand pulls on its own. It's slower to learn, but it stops you scaling a business that only grows while you push.

options.text: Whether sales hit this year's target
options.feedback: A target tells you how much you sold, not why. Growth bought with effort and discounts can hit a target right up until the effort stops.

options.text: What customers say in a satisfaction survey
options.feedback: Useful color, but polite customers often rate you well and never reorder. What they do counts more than what they say.

cards.title: Where the 40% came from.
body: Each number looked fine on its own. Together they said one thing: **every sale was pushed**.

breakdown.label: Closed by Dana
breakdown.detail: New orders came after her own calls and visits

breakdown.label: Average discount
breakdown.detail: Needed to get most deals signed

breakdown.label: Typical sales cycle
breakdown.detail: From first meeting to first order

breakdown.label: Referrals
breakdown.detail: No customer ever sent another one

cards.title: Push without pull
body: When a product doesn't fit its market, **every sale takes about as much effort as the first one**. Growth follows your effort and spending, and it stops when they stop.

Investor Marc Andreessen described this in a 2007 essay. Without fit, he wrote, customers don't quite get the value, word of mouth doesn't spread, sales drag on and many deals never close. With fit, demand starts pulling you instead.

image.label: One figure pushing a heavy cart uphill beside a cart rolling on its own
image.brief: 좌우 비교 일러스트. 왼쪽: 사람이 무거운 수레를 언덕 위로 힘겹게 미는 모습, 라벨 "Push". 오른쪽: 수레가 고객들 손에 끌려 스스로 굴러가는 모습, 라벨 "Pull". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Signs you don't have it yet
body: No single sign proves much. Several together usually do.
list: **Growth tracks effort:** sales rise with your calls or ad spend and fall when you pause
**Sales cycles drag,** and many deals stall
**Every customer wants something different,** so each order becomes custom work
**No word of mouth:** nobody arrives because a customer sent them
cards.callout: The common thread: you're doing the work that customer demand should be doing.
cards.softwareNote: In software, watch for signups that rise and fall with ad spend, trials that only convert after a sales call, and a roadmap shaped by whichever big prospect asked last.

cards.title: A few customers behaved differently.
body: Dana looked at the handful of customers who reordered without being chased. All of them ran cold-storage food warehouses, where cheaper crates cracked in the cold.
Most other customers had bought because of the discount. For them, her crates were nice but not needed. The signs of no fit were real, but they hid a smaller group where something was working.

cards.title: Read the signs in context.
body: Some markets are slow by nature. Selling to hospitals or governments can take a long time even when buyers love the product. Compare signs with your own trend and with similar businesses, not with a fast-moving ideal.
Early on, almost everything needs a push. The worry is a push that never gets lighter as customers pile up.

cards.title: Now it's a chain of gift shops.
body: You own three gift shops and launched your own line of scented candles six months ago. Sales are steady.
Which observation is the strongest sign the candles lack fit?

options.text: Sales jump when staff demo them or run 20% off, then fall back
options.feedback: Sales follow your effort, not demand. That's push without pull. You can keep selling this way, but it won't get easier as you grow.

options.text: Their profit margin is lower than your other products
options.feedback: That's a pricing or cost question. A low-margin product can still be one customers seek out, and a high-margin one can still be pushed.

options.text: Several customers said they love the scent
options.feedback: Kind words are nice but weak evidence. Check whether those customers come back and ask for the candles by name.

cards.title: If every sale feels like the first, you don't have fit yet.
body: Growth that lives only on your effort, discounts and custom work is a warning, however good the totals look.
**Try it today:** list your last ten customers. Mark how many came or reordered without you chasing them.
